slides.0.title: Introducing Chilean wine
slides.0.subtitle: Colonial origins, French varieties and the rediscovery of Carmenère
slides.1.title: From País to French varieties
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The earliest vines
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Wine With Seth records Francisco de Aguirre planting Mission grapes (País) near La Serena in 1551; other sources differ somewhat on the date and the people
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Ochagavía and the 1850s
slides.1.highlights.1.content: In 1851 Silvestre Ochagavía pioneered the introduction of European varieties at Talagante; Chilean producers imported Bordeaux cuttings in the 1850s
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The old houses
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Carmen (1850), Cousiño-Macul (1856), Errázuriz (1870), Santa Rita (1880) and Concha y Toro (1883)
slides.1.content: Chile had colonial País first, then took in Bordeaux varieties in the mid-19th century and founded its old houses.
slides.2.title: The story of Carmenère
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Bordeaux's lost variety
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Carmenère was grown in the Médoc and Graves; phylloxera and a tendency to coulure nearly wiped it out in France (Wikipedia dates phylloxera to 1867, Wine With Seth to 1863)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Mistaken for Merlot
slides.2.highlights.1.content: For most of the 20th century Chileans took it for Merlot ("Merlot selection" or "Merlot Peumal") and often picked and made it together with Merlot
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The 1994 identification
slides.2.highlights.2.content: In November 1994 the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it as a distinct variety at Carmen; Chile's agriculture ministry recognised it officially in 1998
slides.2.content: Carmenère is Chile's defining story: a variety lost in France and misidentified in Chile for a century before being rediscovered.
slides.3.title: Chile today
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Scale
slides.3.highlights.0.content: SAG 2023: 124,436 ha of wine grapes (viníferas); 133,668 ha including pisco grapes
slides.3.highlights.1.title: More red than white
slides.3.highlights.1.content: In 2023 red grapes were 72.8% (90,609 ha) and white 27.2% (33,827 ha)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Area is shifting
slides.3.highlights.2.content: In recent years drought and low grape prices have trimmed planted area, so figures are updated every year
slides.3.content: Chile is a red-led industry whose area is steady but slightly shrinking in recent years.
